property_summary: For any deployed Product C, calling currentVersion() always returns the oracle version with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. equals payoff-transformed oracle().currentVersion()); the mutant returns the raw oracle price so for some oracle prices the returned price differs and the property is violated.

For any oracle implementation and any returned oracle version, the reference product C always returns a currentVersion whose price equals the payoff-transformed oracle().currentVersion().price; the mutant returns the raw oracle price (no transform) and thus differs for inputs where payoffDefinition.transform actually changes the price.

For any oracle-provided OracleVersion, C.currentVersion() always returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition().transform(oracle().currentVersion().price); the mutant returns the raw oracle price so for some oracle prices (those where transform changes the value) the returned price differs.

For any oracle version returned by the product's oracle, C.currentVersion() returns the same OracleVersion but with price = payoffDefinition().transform(oracle().currentVersion().price); the mutant omits this transform and thus will return a different price for any oracle price where transform changes it.

For every oracle price and payoffDefinition, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle version with its price replaced by payoffDefinition().transform(oracle().currentVersion().price); the mutant that omits the transform can return a different price for some oracle-returned prices.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns the oracle provider's version with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. price == payoffDefinition.transform(raw.price)); the mutant returns the raw untransformed price for some oracleVersion, breaking this rule.

For every oracleVersion id, calling c.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition.transform(oracle().atVersion(id).price) (reference); the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some id, so the transformed-equals-raw property can be violated.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the payoffDefinition-transformed price from the oracle; the mutant returns the oracle's raw price for some id and thus can produce a mismatch.

For every oracleVersion id, calling c.atVersion(id) succeeds and returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition.transform(rawOracle.atVersion(id).price); the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some id, so this equality holds for all inputs on the reference but is violated for some input on the mutant.

For every oracleVersion id, c.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals the product payoffDefinition-transformed oracle().atVersion(id).price; the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some id, so this equality holds for the reference for all ids but is violated by the mutant for some id.

For any deployed product C, maintenance() must return the stored maintenance parameter (the value set during initialization); the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() which can differ, so there exist inputs where maintenance() differs.

For any initialized product, maintenance() returns the product's stored maintenance parameter (set at initialize); the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so for some controller.minCollateral() differing from the initialized maintenance the return value will differ.

For any initialized product C, maintenance() always returns the stored maintenance value provided at initialize; the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so when controller.minCollateral() != the initialized maintenance the mutant will return a different value.

For every initialized product, maintenance() returns the maintenance value provided at initialize; the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so when the controller's minCollateral differs from the initialized maintenance the mutant returns a different value.

For any initialized product C, maintenance() returns the stored maintenance value set at initialize; the mutant returns controller().minCollateral() instead, so when the controller's minCollateral() differs from the initialized maintenance the mutant will return a different value (the test fuzzes both values to find such a difference).

For any deployed C, the public positionFee() getter returns the position-fee storage value (which may differ from makerFee); the mutant that reads _makerFee instead will produce a different return for some inputs (when makerFee != positionFee).

For any deployed product C, the public getter positionFee() must always return the stored position-fee slot value (i.e. positionFee() == the value written to the position-fee storage); the mutant that reads the maker-fee slot instead will produce a different return when makerFee() != positionFee(), which the fuzzer can find by supplying two different fee values via initialization.

For any initialized product, the public positionFee() getter must return the stored position-fee value; the mutant that reads the maker-fee slot will return a different value whenever makerFee != positionFee (so there exist inputs that make the mutant differ).

For any initialized product, the public positionFee() getter returns the stored position fee value; the mutant that reads the maker-fee slot returns makerFee instead, so when makerFee != positionFee the mutant returns a different value (violating the rule).

For any initialized product, positionFee() returns the stored position-fee value; the mutant that reads the maker-fee slot will return a different value whenever makerFee != positionFee (so there exist fuzzed initializer fees that make the mutant return a different value).

For every deployed C, makerLimit() must return the stored maker limit value (the value written to the _makerLimit storage slot); the mutant that reads _maintenance instead will return a different value for some inputs (when _makerLimit != _maintenance).
